title: Google Earth risked ruin with retracted AI tool for making fake satellite pics
title_bn: Google Earth risked ruin with retracted AI tool for making fake satellite pics
author: TechPulse
excerpt: “What on earth is Google doing?” Misinformation fears spur walk-back of AI tool.
paragraph1: Previous Ars testing of Google’s SynthID system has shown that Google’s digital watermark can persist despite substantial image edits and data loss. However, Ars also encountered the issue of SynthID limiting image checks to about 10 per day. When Ars prompted Google’s Gemini app to run a SynthID check on several AI-modified images generated within Google Earth—before Google removed the Google Earth feature—Gemini responded that it had “detected digital watermarking indicating that part or all of this image was generated or edited using Google AI tools.
paragraph2: ” But Ess questioned why Google’s policy on preventing the creation of AI-generated images on harmful topics had not stopped him from depicting scenes such as a hospital with a bomb crater in Gaza. He also expressed skepticism about primarily relying on Google’s SynthID watermarking system and Google’s AI tools for verifying whether an image is AI-generated. “Fakes do not travel as clean files with their credentials intact,” Ess wrote.
paragraph3: “They travel as screen recordings, re-encodes, screenshots of screenshots, filmed off somebody’s phone in a hurry.” Indeed, Google’s SynthID was unable to provide any image verification when Ars used a smartphone camera to take a photo of an AI-altered image made using the Google Earth feature. Undermining trust By introducing an AI image generator as a Google Earth feature, Google risked undermining public trust in Google Earth as a reliable reference for providing authentic imagery of the real world, Ess said.
paragraph4: It could have also handed an additional excuse to government officials or anyone who wants to deny genuine satellite photos by claiming they were modified or generated entirely by AI tools. Giving anyone access to an easy tool to create AI-modified satellite imagery could have also made it even harder for journalists and researchers checking misinformation and disinformation. Ess recommended using multiple sources to verify satellite imagery and relying on constantly updated satellite imagery sources such as Europe’s Copernicus Sentinel-2.
paragraph5: Google may have alleviated immediate concerns by deciding to quickly remove the AI tool within Google Earth—but its statement suggested that the company could eventually bring the feature back in the future. “We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies,” according to the Google statement. “So we’re rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails.

title: Here’s the screen you never want to see: One UI 9 permalocking your phone
title_bn: Here’s the screen you never want to see: One UI 9 permalocking your phone
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Saving your curiosity from having to try this on your own phone.
paragraph1: Hadlee Simons / Android AuthorityTL;DR One UI 9 introduces a new security measure that permanently locks your phone after 13 failed unlock attempts. We’ve got a look at the message users will see if they ever cross this unfortunate threshold. There’s no easy button to reset, and users will be forced to restore their phone manually. Samsung’s newest foldables are debuting with One UI 9, and beyond Android 17 itself, that’s introducing a whole lot of little changes.
paragraph2: One important one we highlighted earlier this week concerns device security, and how your phone will now permanently lock itself down after 13 failed attempts to enter a PIN or password. Hopefully that’s never something you have to deal with yourself — but if you’re at all curious what it’s like, we’ve got a hands-on look to share with you.Both Android 17 and One UI 9 are taking steps to harden your phone against attempts to guess its unlock code, adding delays of increasing length after too many attempts before finally locking the device down for good, with no option forward but a full reset.If things ever get that far, here’s the screen you’ll ultimately be presented with, shown off here on a new Galaxy Z Flip 8 (thanks: Dylan H).
paragraph3: Dylan HAs you can see, after 13 failed attempts, Samsung isn’t leaving you with much of an option, instructing users get in touch with Samsung Customer Service for next steps.It might be handy to offer a button for a quick factory reset, but we can certainly understand why Samsung might not want to display such an option. At the very least, there’s a separate setting that just automatically wipes the phone after hitting this threshold:Dylan HWhen that hasn’t been toggled on, though, users with permalocked phones will have no choice but to manually access recovery mode on boot and factory reset the hardware from there.While this is the behavior you can expect from phones launching with One UI 9 like the new foldables, we still have some questions about how this might work for older hardware that will eventually be upgrading.
paragraph4: Samsung’s support docs note that this 13-try policy begins with “devices launched with One UI 9.0,” but doesn’t explicitly clarify if we’ll see the same thing after upgrading from One UI 8.5. We also haven’t been able to find any similar mode for One UI 9 Watch on Samsung’s new wearables.
paragraph5: FollowThank you for being part of our community. Read our Comment Policy before posting.

title: Google nixes its Earth AI feature one day after launch, amid criticism it would spread misinformation
title_bn: Google nixes its Earth AI feature one day after launch, amid criticism it would spread misinformation
author: TechPulse
excerpt: A tool that allowed anyone to generate fake AI-generated imagery and superimpose it over real Google Earth maps quickly spurred backlash.
paragraph1: In Brief Posted: 12:47 PM PDT · July 31, 2026 Image Credits:Google Google rolled out a new feature on Thursday that allowed users to deploy Nano Banana 2, its AI image generator, to create fabricated images inside its satellite imagery mapping app Google Earth. The whole point of this feature, Google said, was to get creative with geography.
paragraph2: But critics quickly pointed out that the tool could be used to create and spread misinformation. The tool, which was prompt-based and allowed pretty much any image to be superimposed over real maps, seemed like a recipe for a deluge of geospatial slop.
paragraph3: “There’s no way that this new AI image generation feature on Google Earth, one of the most reliable sources of visual evidence for journalists and researchers, could possibly be abused to spread misinformation online,” a BBC journalist posted sarcastically Thursday. Now, only a day after the feature’s release, Google has scrapped it.
paragraph4: “We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies,” the company said in a statement. “We’re rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails,” Google added.
paragraph5: The criticism of Google’s tool is understandable, although it’s worth pointing out that, in the age of AI, most imagery that exists on the web can be easily manipulated. You don’t have to be a Photoshop whiz anymore to create semi-credible disinformation; you just need access to an AI image generator, which Google sells, as do many other AI firms.

title_bn: Apple’s new AirTags are back down to their best price
author: TechPulse
excerpt: We spotted a great deal on Tile trackers earlier this week that’s still live, but if you’re an iPhone owner, we ultimately recommend Apple’s latest AirTag. Right now, you can pick up a four-pack for $89 ($10 off) at Amazon and Target, mat
paragraph1: Sheena Vasani writes about tech news, reviews gadgets, and helps readers save money by highlighting deals and product recommendations for The Verge.We spotted a great deal on Tile trackers earlier this week that’s still live, but if you’re an iPhone owner, we ultimately recommend Apple’s latest AirTag. Right now, you can pick up a four-pack for $89 ($10 off) at Amazon and Target, matching the bundle’s all-time low price.
paragraph2: If you’re a member, Costco also has a deal that throws in a fifth AirTag for free.$89A growing number of Bluetooth trackers can tap into Apple’s Find My network these days, but none combine that with Apple’s latest ultra wideband (UWB) chip, which powers even better Precision Finding than before. Precision Finding uses on-screen arrows and distance indicators in the Find My app to guide you directly to a misplaced item, while the second-generation AirTag’s upgraded chip and extended Bluetooth range make it faster and more reliable to locate tags, even in multistory homes.
paragraph3: You can also use Precision Finding to find lost items on an Apple Watch, provided you have a Series 9 or later. And if all else fails, the built-in speaker is noticeably louder than before, making it easier to track down an AirTag by sound.Plus, like its predecessor, the second-generation AirTag comes with a handful of features that are especially useful if you’re traveling this summer.
paragraph4: AirTag sharing lets up to five people keep track of the same item, while Apple’s Share Item Location feature allows you to temporarily share an AirTag’s location with participating airlines, including United, Delta, and American Airlines. It’s still a shame Apple doesn’t include a built-in lanyard hole, meaning you’ll need to buy a separate loop or holder, but the tracker continues to use a replaceable CR2032 battery, so you won’t have to replace the entire device when it eventually runs out of power. And at $89 for a four-pack, it’s also a little easier on your wallet today.

title: Smallest.ai Bags $13 Mn To Build Next-Gen Voice AI Models
title_bn: Smallest.ai Bags $13 Mn To Build Next-Gen Voice AI Models
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Voice AI startup Smallest.ai has raised $13 Mn (around ₹108 Cr) in its Series A funding round led by Seligman…
paragraph1: SUMMARYThe startup plans to deploy the fresh capital to scale its voice AI platform for clients across financial services, healthcare and BPO Voice AI has emerged as one of the hottest segments in the AI space as enterprises turn to voice automation to streamline operations, enhance user experience and trim costs Founded in 2023, Smallest.ai claims to have built low-latency voice AI models that are designed to automate complex workflow operations Voice AI startup smallest.ai has raised $13 Mn (around ₹108 Cr) in its Series A funding round led by Seligman Ventures. The round also saw participation from existing backers Sierra Ventures and 3one4 Capital. The startup plans to deploy the fresh capital to scale its voice AI platform for clients across financial services, healthcare, contact centres and business process outsourcing (BPO). Alongside the investment, the startup also announced the launch of ‘Voice 4.
paragraph2: 0’, a tech framework powered by its in-house architecture Hydra. Unlike traditional voice systems that process tasks sequentially, the startup claims that Hydra handles listening, reasoning and speech generation in parallel. With this, Smallest.ai has raised more than $21 Mn (₹175 Cr) to date. It last raised $8 Mn in its seed round led by Sierra Ventures in October 2025. Founded in 2023 by IIT Guwahati alumni Sudarshan Kamath and Akshat Mandloi, Smallest.
paragraph3: ai claims to have built low-latency voice AI models that are designed to automate complex workflow operations. It counts the likes of TrueCaller, Readymode, Premal and Pocket as clients. Smallest.AI’s platform is built on two major voice models, Pulse STT Pro (speech-to-text) and Lightning V3.1 (text-to-speech), which support 38 languages and feature enterprise capabilities like speaker diarisation, emotion detection and code-switching. Going forward, the startup plans to “significantly” expand its scale over the next year.
paragraph4: It employs around 60 employees, and was also part of the AWS Generative AI Accelerator programme for 2025. Voice AI has emerged as one of the hottest segments within the AI space as enterprises turn to AI-driven voice automation to streamline contact centre operations, enhance customer experience and trim costs. As a result, a growing wave of homegrown startups are launching solutions to cater to this emerging market. In June, Gnani.ai launched its made-in-India Prisma v2.5 STT model with support for 12 languages.
paragraph5: Sarvam AI, too, is gearing up to open up its conversational AI agents platform, Samvaad, to the broader public after an initial enterprise pilot. Meanwhile, Tata Communications and Tata Tele Business Services also recently unveiled a voice AI platform focused on meeting the needs of small and medium businesses.

title: VC-backed startups commit more fraud, and researchers think they know why
title_bn: VC-backed startups commit more fraud, and researchers think they know why
author: TechPulse
excerpt: New research from the U.K.’s Imperial College and France’s Emlyon Business School mapped out how Silicon Valley founders commit fraud — and the role investors play.
paragraph1: A new report from the U.K.’s Imperial College and France’s Emlyon Business School has mapped out the ways Silicon Valley’s VC-backed founders commit fraud — and the role investors play. For the report, published online in June, researchers built a database of tech founders and companies who faced civil and criminal securities fraud prosecutions from the SEC and DOJ between 2000 and 2023. Some famous cases of tech founders being convicted of fraud over the past few years include Frank’s Charlie Javice, Kalder’s Gökçe Güven, Terraform Labs’ Do Kwon, and GameOn’s Alexander and Valerie Lau Beckman. All over X, the tech industry’s social network of choice, the topic of fraud and its gentler word “scam” are discussed, as people debate the limits of ambition and success. “Fraud is much more common and normalized in the startup world than we are ready to admit and accept,” Tim Weiss, one of the authors of the report, told TechCrunch. He pointed to another report from the University of Toronto (UT), also published in June, that looked at 654 fraud cases against U.S.
paragraph2: VC-backed startups from 2000 to 2023. It found that fraud is rare overall but that companies with venture funding were more likely to face fraud charges compared to companies that didn’t take venture funding. It found that startups launched during overheated markets with weak oversight and investor due diligence are 19% more likely to later commit fraud. “The problem here is not just the founders but also those that set and reinforce, at times unreasonable, expectations of high growth,” Weiss said. He added that the current frothy AI startup environment is exactly the kind of conditions that tempt founders into fraud. Weiss’ paper, co-authored with Emlyon researcher Nevena Radoynovska, discusses what may happen when founders face a gap between how investors want their startups to perform and how they are actually performing. They may turn to “façading,” as the paper calls it, in three increasingly dishonest stages: surface, reinforced, and deep. Surface façading is when founders lie about how successful the company is or is becoming. It’s common during the early stages of a company when it’s pitching its vision to investors.
paragraph3: It’s a level of dishonesty higher than just pitching an aspirational vision or an astronomical total addressable market. After the surface façade, the founder may move into “reinforced façading,” according to the paper, which involves creating fake evidence to back up the lies told. The paper gave the example of a mobile testing app that created fake customer contracts and invoices, recorded fake revenue, and used those fake documents to convince VCs to back it at a unicorn valuation. From there founders may enter “deep façading,” where they extend their lies to areas like making their tech seem more capable than it is, complete with fake demos. This involves entire “parallel realities” built on lies, Weiss said. But investors aren’t always hapless victims, the researchers found. Beyond the outsized growth expectations that push founders toward fraud in the first place, some investors unwittingly “co-create fraud,” Weiss said, by continuing to back founders—sometimes the very same ones— who’ve previously been accused of fraud, thereby normalizing it to a certain extent. In fact, the UT report found little evidence that alleged fraud prevents founders from raising funding for new startups, even when those fraud cases received major media attention. “New investors and the broader VC market do not penalize past misconduct,” the UT report said, which is “also consistent with the Silicon Valley culture that embraces failure regardless of the cause.
paragraph4: ” The study also found that startups whose boards were controlled by the founders were twice as likely to commit fraud compared to those with investor-controlled or shared-controlled boards. Even more interesting, it reported that after VC-backed startups go public, they are more likely to face securities class-action lawsuits within two years compared with private equity-backed companies that go public. The fact that companies are staying private longer also contributes. Public companies undergo more scrutiny than private ones. “Founders do not have a professional body or association that could govern or enforce rules of entrepreneurial and investor conduct on how to be a good founder and what reasonable growth expectations are,” Weiss said. Weiss proposes that the SEC routinely investigate and conduct formal audits on startups after they hit a large “investment threshold.” Currently, the SEC typically waits for something like a whistleblower complaint or a lawsuit from investors or former employees to trigger an investigation. Weiss’ paper also suggests that investors should take more accountability when pushing founders to hit extreme growth metrics. “Investors should be held liable for corporate governance failures and violating their fiduciary duties,” he said.
paragraph5: He wants to see more research into “entrepreneur-investor dynamics” that could help prevent fraud and also “balance the overemphasis on the entrepreneur as the sole perpetrator of wrongdoing.” Fraud is rarely a solo act, in other words, and until investors are held to account for the pressure they exert, founders will likely keep facing the temptation to fake it until they make it. title: Zepto To Now Re-Attempt IPO By May 2027: Report
title_bn: Zepto To Now Re-Attempt IPO By May 2027: Report
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Barely a day after reports surfaced that Zepto had deferred its IPO plans, the quick commerce giant’s cofounder and CEO…
paragraph1: SUMMARYCEO Palicha internally told employees said that Zepto will list on the bourses once its financial metrics improve and valuation terms turn more favourable This comes barely a day after the quick commerce giant has put its public listing on the backburner and announced plans to raise about ₹1,000 Cr via a pre-IPO round The CEO also said that Zepto would not have to refile its DRHP from scratch as the startup still has time until November 2027 to list on the stock exchanges Barely a day after reports surfaced that Zepto had deferred its IPO plans, the quick commerce giant’s cofounder and CEO Aadit Palicha has reportedly told employees that the startup is now looking to list on the exchanges in the next two to three quarters. According to Moneycontrol, Palicha, while addressing an employee town hall meeting, said that Zepto will list on the bourses once its financial metrics improve and valuation terms turn more favourable after the aforementioned period. This means that the quick commerce major is now aiming to list on the bourses between February 2027 and May 2027. Addressing the employees, Zepto CEO also reportedly said that the startup would not have to refile its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) from scratch as the startup still has time until November 2027 to list on the stock exchanges. As per the report, Zepto will just file an addendum (updated financials) with markets regulator SEBI to move ahead with its prospective listing plans.
paragraph2: Queries sent to Zepto on the new IPO timeline remained unanswered till the time of publication. This comes barely a day after sources told Inc42 that the quick commerce startup has put its public listing on the backburner. However, the startup now plans to raise about ₹1,000 Cr (around $105 Mn) in a pre-IPO funding round from both domestic and overseas investors. The new IPO timeline comes as Zepto appears to have made no headway with its institutional backers on valuation concerns. Previous reports suggested that the mutual funds were valuing the startup at about $2.
paragraph3: 5 Bn-$3 Bn, significantly below the company’s expectations. The valuation is also less than half of its $7 Bn private market valuation, which it achieved after raising $450 Mn in October 2025. However, the investor scrutiny has not been without reason. As per previous reports, Zepto currently burns over ₹700 Cr of cash each quarter even as competition in the quick commerce landscape shows no signs of letting down. Players in the category continue to spend heavily on dark store networks, discounts and customer acquisition.
paragraph4: On top of this, the startup continues to post heavy losses. Zepto’s net loss widened to ₹5,095 Cr in FY26 from ₹4,697 Cr a year earlier, even as operating revenue nearly doubled to ₹22,624 Cr. Notably, this is not the first time that the Aadit Palicha-led startup has postponed its IPO plans. In June 2025, Zepto first paused IPO plans for a year to cut cash burn and improve profitability. It then once again revived its public listing plans a few months later after filing its DRHP with SEBI in November.
paragraph5: It then received SEBI’s nod and filed its updated DRHP with the markets regulator in July this year. According to its UDRHP, the proposed IPO was to include a fresh issue of up to ₹8,010 Cr and an offer for sale of up to 11.35 Cr shares.

author: TechPulse
excerpt: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is probing nearly 1.2 million Tesla vehicles after receiving complaints about a suspension failure that could cause "a loss of vehicle directional control," as reported earlier by Reuters. Th
paragraph1: Skip to main contentA potential suspension issue could cause ‘a loss of vehicle directional control.’A potential suspension issue could cause ‘a loss of vehicle directional control.’by Emma RothJul 31, 2026, 6:33 PM UTCPhoto by Patrick Pleul/picture alliance via Getty ImagesEmma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
paragraph2: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is probing nearly 1.2 million Tesla vehicles after receiving complaints about a suspension failure that could cause “a loss of vehicle directional control,” as reported earlier by Reuters. The preliminary investigation includes the 2018-2020 Model 3 and 2021-2023 Model Y, according to a filing from the NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation.The NHTSA says it received 156 complaints about the issue, which “involves the detachment of the front lower lateral link.
paragraph3: ” In most cases reviewed by the NHTSA, failure occurred with “no advance warning,” but some “cite noises occurring prior to failure.” The NHTSA hasn’t recorded any crashes, injuries, or fatalities related to the potential issue.This isn’t the first time Tesla dealt with suspension issues. In 2021, Tesla recalled 2,791 Model Y and Model 3 vehicles over a potential suspension defect.

author: TechPulse

paragraph1: Skip to main contentThe company may be releasing its own take on an AirTag-like item tracker.The company may be releasing its own take on an AirTag-like item tracker.by Jay PetersJul 31, 2026, 6:27 PM UTCImage: 9to5GoogleJay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.
paragraph2: Google is seemingly working on an item tracker that might compete with Apple’s AirTag. 9to5Google obtained an image of something called a “Google Pixel Tag” that has a small oval shape. The publication also linked to a Slovenian store listing about the Pixel Tag that describes the gadget as an item tracker with a speaker that uses Google’s “Find My Device” network (which is now called Find Hub).The Pixel Tag is popping up shortly ahead of Google’s planned hardware launch event for August 12th.
paragraph3: Google has already shown off teases of the Pixel 11 lineup for the event, and leaks have also appeared for a new foldable, smartwatch, and earbuds. Earlier this month, 9to5Google noted that early Pixel 11 listings mentioned a Google Pixel Tag but pointed out that “no such tracker exists right now.”Here’s a machine translation of the Pixel Tag’s description from the Slovenian listing:The Google Pixel Tag smart tracker helps you quickly and reliably locate your lost items using the secure “Find My Device” network.Never waste time searching for your keys, wallet or luggage again.
paragraph4: Google Pixel Tag is a compact, lightweight and durable smart tracker that attaches discreetly to your most important items. Using Google’s extensive and secure “Find My Device” network, you can always check the exact location of your belongings via your smartphone. The tracker is equipped with a loud speaker for easy nearby search and is designed with your privacy and personal data in mind.Google didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
